opener.heading: Week 41: Things That Go 🚂
about: Seven days of things that move, and of what makes them move. Azlyn wears a car on Friday, races a numbered fleet down the stairs on Saturday, and spends Sunday finding out that one toy car travels four different distances on four different floors. Monday she hauls the washing the length of the hall. By Thursday the whole house has a single taped road running through it, and every build from the week sits somewhere along it.

Monday is Indigenous Peoples' Day and the afternoon walk goes along the river. One sentence about who lived along that water first is the whole treatment. This week also asks less of her than the last few weeks have, on purpose. The light goes early now, and Thursday joins up what she has already built instead of starting anything new.
azlyn: Predict, then check. She calls the winner out loud before she lets go, and the tape tab on the floor settles it.
The floor does half the work. Six cans dragged on a blanket over carpet, then over bare boards, then the same six in a basket, and the difference arrives through her own arms.
Surfaces change how far things travel. Towel, cardboard, carpet, ice: one car, one ramp, four distances.
Drawing what is in front of her. She draws the same vehicle from memory and then from life, and says what is missing from the first one.
Numbers doing a job. Numbered cars, numbered parking bays, prices in bottle caps, counted back into the jar at the end.
you: Rehearsal teaches something a spontaneous performance can't
A rehearsed thing needs a witness before it is finished
Ice is one of the few materials that changes while she's using it
Heavy pulling settles her faster than any conversation about the noise does
A darkened room helps more than a quiet one
Close looking is the one thing a tired child can still do
Mid-autumn is a low-energy stretch, and lowering the bar is the right response

opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 16 months this week. He stacks four blocks, copies whatever chore he sees you doing, and has ten words or so, which is enough to give him a real job in the middle of every activity Azlyn is running.

days.title: The Car She Wears
days.prepTonight: Empty the biggest box in the house and stand it by the table with the paper plates, the ribbon and the marker on top. Put the craft knife somewhere high.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The First Drive Through the Leaves

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Parking the Car by the Door

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Film of the Practice Run

opening.title: Marking Where the Wheels Go
opening.need: the big box · 1 permanent marker · 5 paper plates.
steps: Stand up the big box you emptied last night, still beside the table, and let her climb into it, which she will do first anyway.
Hold a paper plate flat against the outside while she draws round it with the marker. Four wheels, in the places she picks, even if one ends up near the roof.
The fifth plate is the steering wheel. She marks its spot on the inside front and chooses where the horn goes.

main.title: The Car With No Floor
materials: 1 large cardboard box, deep enough to reach her waist
1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
2 lengths of ribbon or string, about 2 feet each
4 paper plates for the wheels, 1 more for the steering wheel
1 saucepan lid or a bicycle bell for the horn
steps: Cut the base clean out of the box and take the top flaps off, leaving a deep ring she can stand inside. She stands back while you cut, and you tell her why.
Punch two holes in the front edge and two in the back with the point of the knife. Thread a ribbon through each pair, knot it, and tape over the knots inside.
Get her into it. Shorten the ribbons until the box hangs at her waist with her arms free, then tape the slack down.
Tape the four wheels onto her marks and the fifth plate inside the front as the steering wheel.
Hand her the crayons or the paint. Headlights, doors, her name across the back in marker, whatever belongs on it.
Tape the saucepan lid inside beside the steering wheel, or clip the bell onto the front edge.
main.tip: Cut the base out before you cut anything else. She climbed into it at eight o'clock; with the bottom gone she wears it instead.

outside.title: The First Drive Through the Leaves
paras: Take the car onto the wide flat park path and drive it through the leaves the wind brought down. She cannot see her feet in that box, so a drift arrives as sound and drag. Sweep a heap together and let her run through it.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies a bigger person, so he will want a car the minute hers goes on. Tape a paper plate to each side of a shoebox and give it to him. He pushes it, loses it under the sofa, comes back for it.

second.title: Three Runs Before the Show
second.intro: The car has nowhere to go yet, and tomorrow somebody sits down to watch it drive.
materials: 3–4 cushions for the tunnel and the bridge
The saucepan lid horn, taped in this morning
Your phone, to film one run
steps: Tape two parallel lines down the hall to make the road, round the sofa and back to where it started. She picks the route, you tape it.
Lay two cushions flat across the road as the bridge, and stand two more on end with a gap between them as the tunnel.
Six sheets of paper, six signs. She draws each one, you write the word she dictates underneath, and she tapes them along the road at her height.
Run one, start to finish, horn at every sign. Correct nothing.
Ask her what she wants different. Change that one thing, then run it again.
Run three is the filmed one. Hold the phone still and let her drive past you.
Leave the road taped down overnight. It is there in the morning.
second.tip: Three runs is the number. Two and she has not settled in, four and she is bored of her own route.

alternatives: One straight taped line down the hall and nothing else on it.
Strap a doll in as the passenger and drive her about.
Deliver something real on every run: a fork, a sock, a letter.
Park the box car and lay the road out for the toy vehicles.
outAgain: A friend's house, and the car travels in the trunk
The park path, wide and flat and empty on a Friday
A café with a window onto the road, counting what passes
The street where the trash goes out, timed for the garbage truck

aroundWorld.title: Vehicles Everywhere 🚐
paras: Manila runs on jeepneys, long painted buses built out of old army jeeps and decorated by their drivers. Bangkok has the tuk-tuk, three wheels and no doors. Venice has no cars at all, so its buses float: the vaporetto pulls in at the end of the street the way a bus pulls into a curb.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Serve snack off a cart. Load a tray with banana slices and crackers, park it in the hall, and let Azlyn sell to whoever walks past, the way a Manila cart does.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: No two jeepneys are painted the same. Drivers name them and paint the name across the front.

days.krestonPM: At 16 months he has ten words, and this afternoon hands him three: car, beep, gone. Say them as they happen instead of asking him to say them back. Let him thump the saucepan lid once, then take the car off him before he works out that it goes over a head.

insight.headline: Rehearsal teaches something a spontaneous performance can't.
paras: Azlyn drove the same road three times this afternoon and changed one thing in the middle of it. That middle run is where the work sits. A child who repeats a sequence starts to hold the whole shape of it in her head instead of the next step alone, and that frees her up to notice what she wants different. Rehearsal also separates the doing from the being watched, so she gets to be bad at it in private first. By tomorrow the route costs her nothing to drive, which leaves all of her available for the person in the chair.

days.safety: The craft knife is adult-only and goes back onto a high shelf between cuts, not onto the arm of the sofa. A worn box hides her feet and puts her weight off center, so she goes over without ever seeing what caught her. No stairs and no steps in the car, and keep a hand on her anywhere near the curb.

days.title: Race Day
days.prepTonight: Flatten two or three big boxes and stand them by the stairs with the packing tape. Fill a baking tray with water and freeze it for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Fleet on the Starting Line

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Grandstand Made of One Chair

opening.title: The Fleet on the Starting Line
opening.need: every toy vehicle in the house · 1 roll masking tape · 1 permanent marker.
steps: Tip the lot out at the bottom of the stairs and let her line them up however she likes.
Tear a tab of tape for each one, write a number on it, stick it on the roof. She says which car gets which number.
Ask her which number wins. Write her answer on a tab and stick it on the wall.

main.title: The Ramp Down the Stairs
materials: Your phone, for the finish-line photo
steps: Join the flattened boxes into one sheet with the packing tape, seams underneath.
Lay it over the bottom three or four treads and weight the top edge with the two heavy books.
A strip of masking tape across the top is the start line. Nothing gets a push.
Release the cars one at a time. Where each stops, stick down a tab of masking tape with its number on it in marker.
Crouch at the foot of the ramp, off the cardboard, and look along the spread with her. Ask her which went furthest and whether it matches the number on the wall.
Photograph the floor with the tabs in shot, then let her run it again with the three she liked best.
main.tip: She will shove them, which makes her arm the experiment instead of the car. Hold it on the line, count to three, lift your finger. She copies the count.

outside.title: Acorns Down the Slide
paras: Fill a pocket with acorns under the oaks and take them to the slide. Send them down two at a time and call the winner before they land. Acorns roll, buckeyes roll faster, and a flat leaf goes nowhere at all. Sweep the slide clear when you leave so nobody sits on a handful.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and stacks four blocks now, so he builds as well as flattens. Give him four cars of his own at the far end of the room, well clear of the run-out, and let him pile them into a heap he can knock over. At the park he takes the short toddler slide on his own, sitting up and feet first, with you standing at the bottom to catch him, and never on your lap. The acorns stay in your pocket and he sends a leaf down instead.

second.title: The Grandstand Made of One Chair
second.intro: One chair turns the stairs into a race meeting, and the person in it is the whole crowd.
materials: The stair ramp and the numbered fleet
The box car and the saucepan lid horn
A propped-up phone, if the guest is a video call
steps: Set the chair beside the ramp, out of the run-out, with one person in it. A grandparent on a propped-up phone counts.
Tickets first. She folds a sheet of paper, draws a car on it, and hands it over at the door.
Re-lay the start line with masking tape and set the ramp up as it stood this morning.
She announces each car by its number before she lets it go. Give her the words once (car number three, on the line), then stop feeding them.
Write the finishing order on the remaining paper with the marker as she calls it out.
The audience of one claps every car, including the ones that stall halfway. Say so before the first race.
Last event is her lap in the box car, down the hall and back, horn past the chair.
second.tip: Leave the chair where it is. The ramp is up by then, so at 4:15 she runs the fleet along the floor and into the shoebox past the empty chair, and that showing is hers.

alternatives: Two cars only, best of five, and stop.
Build a garage at the foot of the ramp for the finishers.
Line the fleet up by size, then color, then speed.
Draw the race and post it to whoever could not come.
outAgain: The fire station, or a field edge where the tractors are lifting the last of the crop
The garage forecourt from a safe distance, watching the lifts and the air line
The park, for the slide with the acorns still in her pocket
A bus ride to the end of the route and back, in the front seats right behind the driver
days.krestonPM: He is 16 months and copies chores, so give him a real one out of the house: his own small bag to carry in and out. Back home he sits on a knee in the grandstand chair for two races. He claps when the clapping starts, a beat late and with his whole arms.

insight.headline: A rehearsed thing needs a witness before it is finished.
paras: Azlyn drove her road three times yesterday for nobody, and this morning she has been waiting for the chair to be filled. Rehearsal gets the thing built; a witness closes it. Children this age treat an audience as part of the work rather than a reward at the end of it, which is why she keeps checking your face mid-race and why the same fleet run alone on the floor has a different feel for her. One person facing her, doing nothing else, does the whole job. A crowd of six splits into six half-attentions and she can feel it. A grandparent on a propped-up phone counts, which is worth knowing on a Saturday when nobody can come round.

days.safety: Cardboard taped over stair treads is a slip hazard for everybody in the house. It comes up the moment you stop racing, and nobody uses those stairs while it is down. The box-car lap stays in the hall, and the cardboard comes off the treads before she puts the car on. Hard vehicles leave the foot of the ramp fast, at Kreston's head height when he is sitting, so keep him off to the side or behind a door.

days.title: The Ice Road
days.prepTonight: The tray of ice stays in the freezer until 9:15. Put four or five shoeboxes, two old towels and a sheet of stiff card by the table.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Three Roads and One in the Freezer

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Parking Garage Made of Shoeboxes

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Last of the Ice in the Sink

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: A Warm Bath After a Cold Morning

opening.title: Three Roads and One in the Freezer
opening.need: 1 bath towel · 1 piece of flattened cardboard · a bare patch of carpet · 1 toy car.
steps: Lay the towel and the cardboard side by side on the carpet. Three roads, running next to each other.
She pushes the car across each one and tells you which is fastest. Take her answer without arguing it.
Tell her there is a fourth road in the freezer and keep the door shut.

main.title: Four Surfaces, One Car
materials: 1 baking tray of water, frozen overnight
1 sheet of stiff card, 2 books to prop it
steps: Prop the stiff card on the two books and tape the bottom edge down so the slope holds all morning.
Lay the bath towel at the foot of the ramp and send the car down. Tab where it stops with masking tape, marked TOWEL in permanent marker.
Swap in the cardboard, run it, tab it CARD. Then bare carpet, run it, tab it CARPET.
Bring the ice tray out, set it at the foot of the ramp on the two old towels, and run the car onto it. It overshoots every other tab in the room, so tab that one ICE.
Walk the four tabs with her and let her say which road won. She will want the ice again, so let her.
Leave the ice out under her hands and run the car every ten minutes. As it goes soft the distance walks back towards the carpet tab.
main.tip: Narrate rather than quiz. The ice is going soft, look how short that one was hands her the words while she works.

outside.title: Two Sticks Off the Bridge
paras: Take two sticks each to whatever bridge you can walk to, drop them off the upstream side together, and run to the other rail to see whose arrives first. October water runs quick and full of leaves, so half of them snag. Pick sticks of different sizes and let her call the winner before the drop.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies whatever he sees done, so he wants a stick the second one goes over. Hand him his own, keep a fist in the back of his coat at the rail, and let him watch it drop. In and gone are two of his ten words, and this is what they look like.

second.title: The Parking Garage Made of Shoeboxes
second.intro: Every car in the house gets a numbered bay this afternoon, in a building that comes out of the recycling.
materials: 1 ruler or a straight strip of card
steps: Lay the shoeboxes on their sides with the open ends out, two on the bottom row and the rest stacked above. Tape each joint as you go.
Cut the first ramp from the flattened cardboard with the scissors while she holds the tower steady.
Tape it from the floor below to the lip above and test it with one car. Cut the next only once that one runs.
Rule the bays. Hold the ruler across each floor and let her draw the lines with the marker, counting as they appear.
Number every bay. She calls the numbers, you write them, and the ones that come out backwards stay backwards.
Park the whole fleet, one car per bay. Anything left over lines up on the ramp.
Take one car off the bottom row and let her drive it up and out through every floor.
second.tip: Build the bottom row wide. Two boxes under one carries the whole afternoon, and she will lean on it.

alternatives: One shoebox, one ramp, one car.
Park by color instead of number.
Draw a parking lot on a flattened box and tape the bays out.
Fill the sink with the last of the ice and leave her to it.
outAgain: A nature hunt walk, with a bag for buckeyes, acorns and the reddest leaf
The riverside path, to see where the morning's sticks ended up
Feed the ducks and count what floats past
A playground with a metal slide, cold enough now to be interesting
days.krestonPM: He stacks four blocks at 16 months, so give him two spare shoeboxes of his own at the other end of the table. He builds up, knocks it down, builds up again. Keep the fleet out of his half; he will put a car in his mouth inside a minute.

insight.headline: Ice is one of the few materials that changes while she's using it.
paras: Most of what Azlyn plays with sits still and waits. Ice does not. It is slippery, then wet, then a puddle with a lump in it, and the change runs on a clock she can feel inside one activity. That hands her something few toys do: a before and an after she caused part of, with her own warm hands in the middle of it. Children hold on to sequences they have watched the whole way through. Say the stages out loud as they pass and the vocabulary of change (melting, softer, gone) arrives attached to a thing in her hands.

days.safety: Melt water spreads further than you expect and a hard floor gets dangerous fast, so keep the old towels down and mop between runs while Kreston is walking. Ice straight out of the freezer sticks to skin, so let the block sit a minute before she handles it. Single toy cars are choke-sized for him, so the fleet goes back up on the table between runs. Buckeyes and acorns are the same size in his mouth, and a chewed buckeye poisons a child, so the hunt bag stays on your shoulder and Kreston carries leaves and nothing else. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Moving Day
days.prepTonight: Leave the dirty washing in the basket instead of the machine, and stand the basket, the rope and a roll of masking tape by the hall door.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Taping the Track Down the Hall

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Two Ways to Shift the Same Load

opening.title: Taping the Track Down the Hall
steps: Run two lines of masking tape down the hall, a stride apart. She walks between them to check the width.
Cushions along the track at intervals, one per station. She puts them where she wants them.
Ask what each station is called. Hold the names in your head, because she writes them at 9:15.

main.title: The Hallway Railway
materials: 6 feet of rope or a bathrobe belt
Paper and 1 marker for the station signs
Real cargo: the washing, a bag of cans, a stack of books
1 wooden spoon and 1 saucepan for the whistle
steps: Tie the rope to the front of the basket and put the free end in her hand. She is the engine, the basket is the wagon.
Mark each station with a cross of masking tape beside its cushion, so the stops stay put once the cushion gets kicked.
One sign per station. She draws, you write the name she gave you underneath, and each sign leans on its cushion.
Load the washing and haul it to the station nearest the machine. It comes out of the basket and waits by the door.
Second run, the cans to the cupboard. Third run, the books to the shelf. Every trip carries something that had to move anyway.
Bang the wooden spoon on the saucepan at each station. She will want that job, so hand it over on run two.
main.tip: Real cargo is the whole difference. A basket of nothing gets abandoned at station two. A basket with the cans in gets dragged the length of the house four times.

outside.title: The Barrow Full of Leaves
paras: Rake the leaves off the path into one heap, load them into a wheelbarrow, a laundry basket or two grocery bags, and let her wheel the lot to wherever they go. She will tip half of it out on the way and want to jump in the rest, both of which are fine. Load it twice.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, which is the whole job description this morning. Give him a small bag and let him carry leaves from the heap to the barrow, one fistful per trip. He will do it for longer than you expect, and the walking-while-carrying is the part he is working on.

second.title: Two Ways to Shift the Same Load
second.intro: Six cans weigh the same whatever they travel on. Her arms are about to tell her something else, and finding that out is worth the afternoon.
materials: 6 heavy things: cans, books, a bag of potatoes
1 roll masking tape for the finish line
A stretch of carpet and a stretch of bare boards or vinyl, whichever the house has
A stopwatch, or the timer on your phone
steps: Tape a finish line across the far end of the hall, and a second one the same distance down the carpeted room. Each course starts at a door.
Pile the six heavy things onto the blanket. Cans, books, potatoes, all of it.
She takes a corner and drags it the length of the carpet. Start the timer and say the number out loud when she crosses the tape.
Same blanket, same load, down the hall boards this time. Time it again. The floor changed and nothing else did.
Move the same load into the basket, tie the rope back on, and send her down the hall again. Time that too.
Ask her which was hardest, take her answer as it comes, then ask what the basket does for her that the blanket does not.
Let her load it herself and run it as often as she likes. Stop timing once she stops asking, and on the last run she sits in the basket and you pull. She has earned that.
second.tip: Load it heavy enough that the blanket run is hard work. A light load slides fine on anything and teaches her nothing.

alternatives: One journey, one basket, one heavy thing.
Drag the blanket with a doll on it and nothing else.
Move every book in the house to a new shelf.
Pull each other up and down the hall and stop there.
outAgain: The riverside path, and today is Indigenous Peoples' Day, so tell her in one sentence who lived along this water first
The neighborhood park, kicking through whatever the wind brought down
The woods loop, hunting for the first bare tree
A walk to the recycling bins with everything the railway carried
days.krestonPM: He has ten words at 16 months and more is often one of them, so give it something to attach to: put one can in the basket, pull him two steps, stop. He asks. You go again. That exchange is worth more to him this afternoon than the ride is.

insight.headline: Heavy pulling settles her faster than any conversation about the noise does.
paras: A child kept indoors on a wet October Monday gets loud, clumsy and quick to cry. She needs pushing, pulling and carrying to feel where her limbs are, and a warm carpet gives her nothing to push against. Hauling a basket of cans the length of the hall delivers that load through her shoulders, hips and hands, which is why she comes back down after it and why an hour of screen time leaves her worse. Talking to her about the volume asks the part of her that is already flooded to do more work. Give her something heavy to move first, then say the thing you were going to say.

days.safety: The rope stays in a hand, hers or yours, and goes back in the drawer the moment you stop, never left slack or in a loop on the floor. A loaded basket dragged down a hallway does not stop for a 16-month-old, so Kreston rides in the basket or waits behind a door, never underfoot. Socks on taped floorboards slide, so put her in bare feet.

days.title: Headlights
days.prepTonight: Find the flashlight, check it works and check the battery cover is screwed shut. Put the foil, the cereal-box card and the tape beside it.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Signs That Catch the Light

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Reflector Hunt on the Curb

opening.title: The Signs That Catch the Light
opening.need: kitchen foil · 4 pieces of cereal-box card · 1 roll masking tape · 1 permanent marker.
steps: She tears the foil into rough patches, shiny side up, and tapes one onto each piece of card.
Marker on top of the foil: an arrow, a cross, a circle, whatever a road sign means to her.
Stand the four signs along the baseboard at the height of a toy car and put no light on them yet.

main.title: The Headlight Test
materials: 1 flashlight, plus your phone flashlight as backup
The four foil signs from this morning
1 blanket or towel for the window
The fleet and the box car
steps: Clear the floor of everything that is not a car, then tape the blanket over the window and shut the door.
Hand her the flashlight. The fleet is at the far end of the room and she finds it with the beam.
Hold the flashlight low, at the height of a car's own headlights, and drive one car up the room. Then hold it high and look at what changed.
Point the beam at the foil signs from across the room. The foil throws it straight back, and she will say so before you do.
Make two more on the spot: spare card, a patch of foil taped on, a shape in marker. She stands them where she wants and tests them from the door.
Put her in the box car with the flashlight and let her drive the dark room. Your phone flashlight is the streetlight, on the floor, pointing up.
main.tip: Give her the flashlight and keep your hands off it. Half of what she is learning is that the beam goes where she points.

outside.title: The Reflector Hunt on the Curb
paras: The clocks go back at the start of November and the light is going by half past six, so spend this one counting what is built to be seen in the dark. Bike pedals, the reflectors on a trash can left out for pickup, the strip on a mail carrier's coat, the red plastic on the back of every parked car. She finds five before you turn for home.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, and the light switch is the chore he wants most. Hold him up to it and let him work it: on, off, on. Say the words with the flick rather than after it, because he is matching sound to event all day.

second.title: The Tunnel Under the Table
second.intro: The dark space under the dining table has been catching her eye all week. Two blankets over the top turn it into somewhere she drives through and then stays.
materials: 2 dark blankets or a duvet cover
A snack and a drink in a lidded cup
steps: Drape both blankets over the table with two opposite ends left open. That is the tunnel.
Clip the blankets to the table legs with the clothespins so it survives being crawled through.
Cushions down the middle as the floor, leaving a clear run for the cars.
She drives the fleet in one end and out the other by flashlight, one car at a time.
Send a car in and let her find it with the beam from outside. Then she hides one for you.
Snack and the lidded cup go in. Eating under a table is most of the appeal.
Four books in and the flashlight on. Read one lying down, then leave her in there.
second.tip: Take the tunnel with you to the pool as a promise. She comes out of the water quicker when there is somewhere to go back to.

alternatives: One blanket over two chairs and stop there.
Flashlight shapes on the ceiling from her back.
Drive the fleet through a row of shoeboxes with the ends cut out.
Read in the dark and skip the cars.
outAgain: Swimming
The pool's quiet hour if the after-school crowd is in
Indoor playground, if the pool is shut for a school session
A bath with the lights off and the flashlight on the side, if nobody has the energy
days.krestonPM: At 16 months he walks and stands on his own, which changes what the pool asks of him. Keep a hand on him on the tiles, hold him upright in chest-deep water and let him march on the bottom. Twenty minutes and out, wrapped up before he cools.

insight.headline: A darkened room helps more than a quiet one.
paras: Azlyn gets wound up and nothing lands, so you take the noise down. Try the light instead. Vision takes the biggest share of what her brain is handling, and dropping the room to one flashlight beam cuts most of that input at a stroke, which is why a fort, a tunnel or a parking lot under a blanket settles her inside five minutes. The beam also gives her one thing to attend to and permission to ignore the rest. Anything that has to be talked through goes better under a table with a flashlight than at a bright kitchen table.

days.safety: Small flashlights and bike lights run on button batteries, and a swallowed one burns through a child's throat within hours. Check that every light you hand her has a battery cover screwed shut, and keep loose batteries off the floor. Clear the floor before you darken the room, and keep the box car on the level and nowhere near the stairs while it is dark, because it hides her feet. Keep the table blanket clipped where Kreston cannot pull it down onto himself. Reflectors live at the curb, so Kreston walks on your hand or rides with the stroller brake on, Azlyn stays on the house side of you, and you both stop at every driveway to look before you cross it. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Slow Look
days.prepTonight: Clear the table, put out the paper, the pencils and the crayons, and pick one vehicle out of the fleet to be tomorrow's model. Find the library card.

opening.title: Every Part She Can Name
opening.need: 1 toy vehicle · 1 sheet of paper · 1 pencil.
steps: Put the vehicle you picked from the fleet last night in her hands and ask her to name one part of it. Write every word she gives you down the sheet as she says it.
She will run dry at about six. Turn the vehicle over and let her find three more underneath.
Read the list back to her in her own words. Leave it on the table beside where she draws at 9:15.

main.title: The Car She Draws Twice
materials: 1 magnifying glass, or a jam jar of water
Masking tape, to hold the paper down
steps: Tape a sheet of paper down in front of her and put the vehicle out of sight. She draws it from memory, and you say nothing at all while she works.
Write MEMORY on the back in pencil and set it aside face down.
Stand the vehicle on the table where she can see it, tape down a second sheet, and let her draw it again with the real thing in front of her.
Hand her the magnifying glass, or stand the jam jar of water behind a wheel so it swells. Give her the tread, the axle, the seam down the middle of the roof.
Third sheet, wheels only, as big as the paper goes. Nothing else on the page.
Lay the first two side by side and let her tell you what is on one and missing from the other. Write her sentence under the second drawing word for word.
main.tip: Resist naming the parts she has left out. She finds them through the glass, and a part she found stays hers.

outside.title: Counting Wheels From a Bench
paras: Take the nearest bench to a road and sit on it for twenty minutes with nothing to do but count wheels. Cars have four, bikes have two, the stroller has four small ones, and the garbage truck has more than either of you can count from a bench. She will want to run after ten minutes, so walk a loop and come back to the same bench for a second sitting.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and points at what he wants named, so a bench by a road keeps him busy. Say the whole word back with one more attached (a bus, a red bus). At ten words and climbing, his half of the exchange is the point, so leave gaps he can fill.

second.title: The Spotting Book
second.intro: She has drawn the same vehicle three times today. Now she makes a book with a different one on every page, small enough to go in a bag and out of the house.
materials: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half
1 stapler (you hold it), or string and a pencil to punch the holes
1 small bag she carries it in
steps: Fold the three sheets together in half and let her run her thumb down the crease.
Staple the fold three times while she holds the pages square, or punch two holes with the pencil point and tie the string through.
One vehicle per page. She draws them all: car, bus, truck, bike, tractor, whatever she saw from the bench.
Caption each page in her words with the marker, underneath the drawing. Her spelling and her grammar, not yours.
Leave the last page blank for something she has not seen yet, and tell her that is what it is for.
Book in the bag, pencil in the bag, and walk to the library. She ticks a page every time one goes past.
At the library, find a book with the vehicle she could not draw in it, and borrow that one.
second.tip: Keep the book in the bag by the door all week. It goes out with you tomorrow, and the ticks are what make it hers.

alternatives: One page, one vehicle, and stop.
Cut pictures out of a catalog and stick them in instead.
Make the book about doors, or hats, or dogs.
Skip the book and tick things off a list on the way to the library.
outAgain: The library, every two weeks, and the spotting book goes in
Indoor playground, if the library has a session on and it is packed
The park on the walk home, with the book still in the bag
A café with a window, ticking what goes past over a bun
days.krestonPM: He is 16 months and copies chores, so let him hand his own book over at the desk. Board books are for chewing at his age and the library knows it. Sit him in the picture-book corner and let Azlyn choose his for him, which she will take more care over than choosing her own.

insight.headline: Close looking is the one thing a tired child can still do.
paras: Some days Azlyn has nothing in the tank for building, running or being reasonable, and a magnifying glass and one object will still hold her for twenty minutes. Looking hard asks almost nothing of her body and a good deal of her attention, which is the ratio a flat day needs. It also feeds the thing her drawing is short of: children draw what they know rather than what is in front of them, and the only route from one to the other runs through looking at the real thing for longer than feels necessary. Keep the glass in the kitchen drawer.

days.safety: The bench sits at a curb, so Kreston walks on your hand or rides with the stroller brake on, Azlyn sits on the house side of you, and neither of them steps off the sidewalk after a wheel. The walk to the library goes the same way. The stapler stays in your hand and goes back in the drawer the moment the book is bound, and any staple that misses gets picked off the floor before Kreston is down there. Single toy cars are choke-sized for him, so the model vehicle stays on the table and out of his reach. A jam jar of water is glass, so stand it well in from the table edge.

days.title: Everything Joins Up
days.prepTonight: Carry the week's builds into one room: the parking garage, the foil signs, the station cushions and the box car, with the masking tape on top.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: One Road Through the Whole House

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Cargo Run to the Big Tree

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Shop at the End of the Road

opening.title: Emptying the Garage
opening.need: the parking garage · the fleet · 1 spare shoebox.
steps: The shoebox parking garage from Sunday came in last night with the rest of the week's builds. Take every car out of it and line them up on the floor.
Count them into the spare shoebox out loud, one at a time. Let her lose count and start again.
Ask where each one needs to get to today. The road you build at 9:15 has to reach all of them.

main.title: One Road Through the Whole House
materials: The week's builds: the parking garage, the foil signs, the station cushions, the box car
steps: Start at the parking garage. Tape two lines out of its bottom ramp, a car's width apart, running towards the first station cushion.
Where the road meets a doorstep or a gap, cut a bridge from the cardboard offcuts and tape it flat at both ends.
Keep going to the box car's parking bay and on to the end of the hall. One rule and it is hers to enforce: every vehicle reaches every place.
She drives one car the whole length and mends the road wherever it stops rather than starting again.
Stand Tuesday's foil signs at the junctions, taped to the baseboard.
Last, the paper and the marker. One sign for each place the road reaches, named as she says it.
main.tip: Let her enforce the rule on you. A road that goes everywhere is a rule she can hold in her head, and she catches the dead ends first.

outside.title: The Cargo Run to the Big Tree
paras: Walk the year's route to its biggest tree and make that the depot. Stop where you took January's photograph and take the autumn one from the same spot, third of the four. She carries the cargo (buckeyes, two apples, the spotting book) to the trunk, then loads whatever the tree has dropped and hauls it home.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and carries things while he walks, which is most of what he is practicing. Give him one big leaf for the walk to the tree. He arrives with it, shows you, and drops it. Bring a spare. The buckeyes stay in the bag with you, because every one of them is a choking size at 16 months.

second.title: The Shop at the End of the Road
second.intro: A shoebox on its side at the far end of the hall gives the road somewhere to deliver to, and her a reason to drive it forty times.
materials: Paper, 1 marker and 1 roll masking tape
20 bottle caps or buttons as the coins
1 jar with a lid, for the coins
1 toy truck, or a small box on wheels
6 cans and boxes from the cupboard
Washable poster paint and 1 wide soft brush
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
steps: Set the shoebox on its side at the far end of the road. She writes the shop's name on paper with the marker and tapes it up, then stocks it from the cupboard: six real cans and boxes, arranged how she wants them.
Price each one in bottle caps. One cap, two caps, three. Her prices, and they make no sense.
Load the truck at the parking garage end and drive the delivery the length of the road. Unload, restock, go again.
Swap over. You shop, she serves, and she counts the coins into her hand out loud.
Get the pad out. She dictates the shopping list for the 2:30 trip and you write every item she says, including the ones you will not be buying.
Count the bottle caps back into the jar before you leave and put the lid on.

The October handprint sheet comes out last. Kreston goes on it first while he is calm, the washcloth already in your other hand. Then Azlyn on the same sheet beside him. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write October, her 3 and his 16 months beside the pair. If you are marking the frame this month, this is the afternoon for it: both of them against the door frame, a pencil line each, with the name and the date beside it.
second.tip: Buy one thing off her list at the store, whatever it is. She spends the trip watching to see whether her list counted.

alternatives: Shop only, no road, on the kitchen table.
Deliver to three shops instead of one.
Sort the cupboard cans into a shop, no toys.
Draw the road as a map on the back of a cereal box.
outAgain: The grocery store, with her list in her hand and one thing on it that is hers to find
The bakery, and she pays with a real coin
The market, if it runs on a Thursday
A walk to the mailbox with a letter she dictated
days.krestonPM: He copies chores at 16 months, so give him the lightest real job in the store: one packet to hold from the shelf to the cart. He will carry it the whole way round. At home he hands things up to Azlyn while she puts the shopping away.

insight.headline: Mid-autumn is a low-energy stretch, and lowering the bar is the right response.
paras: The run from the end of the light to the clocks changing is the flattest of the year for small children, and Azlyn is in the back half of it. The light drops, the first colds arrive, and the novelty of the season has gone. A three-year-old in that stretch does less, asks to be carried more and comes apart over a sock. Halving the plan is the accurate response rather than the lazy one: she gets the same hours with you and fewer demands inside them. Today joins up things she already built and asks almost nothing new of her. Do that on purpose.

days.safety: Bottle caps and buttons are the exact size that blocks a 16-month-old's airway. The coins come out only while you are at the store counter with them, and they get counted back into the jar and onto a high shelf before Kreston is loose in the room. The scissors stay with you.
